newsitem.title: UK: Amnesty condemns widespread "torture" in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty condemns widespread "torture" in Russia.

text.p: Amnesty International on Thursday condemned what it called the systematic and widespread use of torture by law enforcement bodies in Russia and said President Boris Yeltsin was partly to blame.
The London-based human rights organisation issued a report detailing cases of alleged torture of suspects and prisoners and urged the Russian government to stamp out the practice.
"Torture occurs every day and everywhere -- anyone could be subject to torture in Russia," Mariana Katzarova, author of the report, said.

"Torture happens in police custody, in pre-trial detention, prisons and the army," she told a news conference, saying that the homeless and members of ethnic minorities such as Chechens faced the greatest risk.
"Why does the Russian government, knowing people have been tortured, do nothing to stop these brutal acts?" she said.

Katzarova said Yeltsin had exacerbated the situation by signing three decrees to boost the fight against organised crime which allowed suspects to be held incommunicado for 30 days instead of the 48 hours as laid down by law.
"I am very much concerned that the president has allowed himself to violate the constitution by issuing decrees and by keeping them in place for years," she said.
Russia committed itself to outlawing torture last year when it signed the European Convention on Human Rights but Katzarova said little had changed for the better.
Common forms of torture included the slonik', or elephant, where a suspect was chained to a chair and had a gas mask put over their head.

Police would then either cut off the air supply until the suspect started suffocating or spray tear gas into the mask. Katzarova said the practice was particularly common in Mordovia, a region just east of Moscow.
Another kind of abuse was the lastochka', or swallow, where a prisoner had his or her hands tied behind their back before being suspended from the ceiling and beaten.
Amnesty said it would raise the mattrer with Russian embassies around the world as well as through the 40-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The report also described conditions of detention in Russia as "amounting to torture". Amnesty said it had received reports that prisoners had died from overcrowding, lack of oxygen and unsanitary prison conditions.

It cited an example from July 1995 when 11 prisoners died of heat stroke in the Siberian city of Novokuznetsk, where 25 people were being held in cells meant for 10 and the temperature rose as high as 48 to 51 Celsius (118 to 124 Fahrenheit).

Katzarova said there were reports that Yeltsin's human rights commission had begun to take an interest in the matter. "This gives me hope that although no practical steps are being taken, at least government officials are starting to talk about the problem," she said.
The Amnesty report also documented the use of torture and ill-treatment by both sides of the armed conflict in Chechnya, including the use of electric shock torture and rape.
The brutal hazing of army conscripts, blamed for scores of deaths each year, also showed no signs of abating, it said.
